abstract.p: Learning to solve a complex task involves discovering new concepts and understanding how to use them. Here, we studied how these two aspects of learning should be sequenced to promote effective task acquisition. We designed video games in which different concepts (tools or ingredients) were used sequentially to complete the task (reach a goal or create a potion). During self-directed learning, participants chose to progress via a curriculum that graduated the complexity of concept discovery (number of concepts involved) rather than of concept implementation (number of steps to goal). However, those who chose to graduate the implementation complexity performed better. Seven subsequent experiments that randomised participants into curriculum groups confirmed that adjusting the complexity of concept implementation (not discovery) is the more effective learning strategy. When acquiring complex tasks, learners should not attempt to discover new concepts prematurely, but instead focus on practicing those which they have already mastered.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Concepts are the building blocks of our mental models. They help us organize knowledge about the world and deploy this knowledge for effective goal-directed actions. The two challenges of discovering new concepts and using them purposively have long been considered twin cornerstones of cognition (Pylyshyn, 1973). Concept learning is a central theme across disciplines, each bringing a unique perspective: psychologists and neuroscientists have studied the development and neural underpinnings of mental representations (Carey, 2011; Frankland & Greene, 2020; Murphy, 2002), education researchers have focused on techniques for expanding knowledge and correcting misconceptions (Vosniadou, 2009), and AI researchers have examined how distributions and sequences of training data determine transfer of machine performance (Bengio et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2021). Over half a century of research has identified robust principles that improve learning outcomes: retrieval practice (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006), spacing (Cepeda et al., 2006), interleaving (Avrahami et al., 1997; Carvalho & Goldstone, 2014; Dekker et al., 2022), and desirable difficulties (E. L. Bjork & Bjork, 2011b; Kirk-Johnson et al., 2019). However, this work has largely focused on simple tasks, such as categorizing stimuli, memorizing word pairs, or practicing isolated problem types. We thus lack a systematic understanding of the curricula that promote concept learning in richer, more naturalistic scenarios.

In this paper, we studied the curricula (ordered sequences of training items) that promote successful learning of complex tasks in human adults. A fundamental tenet of curriculum design is that learners should ‘start small’ by tackling simple problems before moving on to more elaborate ones (Elman, 1991; Krueger & Dayan, 2009; Skinner, 2019; Zhao et al., 2023). However, tasks can differ in both (1) the complexity of concept discovery (the range or intricacy of different concepts that must be grasped to solve the problem) and (2) the complexity of concept implementation (the number of steps needed to reach a goal). For example, solving an equation might require several different concepts to be grasped (e.g. factorisation, substitution, cancellation), and also demand multiple algebraic operations to be performed in sequence. A successful curriculum for mastering algebra might involve first grasping the full range of relevant concepts for single step problems, before progressing to equations involving multiple operations (below, we call this a ‘discovery-first’ curriculum). Conversely, the most effective curriculum might first train problems of increasing depth (one-step, two-step, n-step) for a single concept, before progressing to learn a wider set of additional concepts (an ‘implementation-first’ curriculum). In between these extremes, there exists an almost limitless space of potential curricula in which the difficulty of concept discovery and implementation are sequenced in more intricate ways. The goals of the current research were (1) to understand the principles by which these curricula promote successful concept learning, and (2) to study whether participants adopt these principles when allowed to design their own curriculum in a self-directed learning setting.

In tackling this question, we build on foundational work that has examined the factors that promote memorisation and skilled performance. Encoding into long-term memory is facilitated when learners use their knowledge in an interim test (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006) and engage more deeply with a study item (Craik & Lockhart, 1972). We also draw on empirical and computational research, showing that the order in which concepts are encountered during learning shapes the representations that are ultimately acquired (Zhao et al., 2023; Dekker et al., 2022), including work on blocking vs. interleaving in category learning (Avrahami et al., 1997; Carvalho & Goldstone, 2014), and findings that making learning more effortful, for instance through spacing study sessions (E. L. Bjork & Bjork, 2011b; Zechmeister & Shaughnessy, 1980) and alternating learning material (Kirk-Johnson et al., 2019; Rohrer & Taylor, 2007), leads to better outcomes. However, we take a different approach to earlier studies. Instead of using a standard behavioral paradigm, we created an interactive computer game that involved navigating a grid world to reach a goal (Fig. 1a). The game was designed to be rich and engaging, whilst also affording us tight control over the complexity of concept discovery and implementation. It was also procedurally generated, so that participants could not memorize trajectories or heuristics but had to grasp and use concepts in a generalizable fashion (Allen et al., 2024). Reaching the goal required participants to move from room to room using one to four different tools (which we equate with concepts), and trajectories to the goal could involve between one and four steps. This approach allowed us to create a 4 x 4 grid of complexity levels that systematically varied the difficulty of concept discovery and implementation. We defined a curriculum as a trajectory through this 2D grid that unfolded over a fixed number of training trials. Despite involving only 16 levels and 48 trials, our simple set up afforded over 1057 distinct possible curricula. This allowed us to ask which curriculum features would promote successful learning, measured by performance on a later, independent test phase.

We systematically charted the principles underlying successful curriculum learning for concept discovery and implementation across eight experiments. First, we asked which curricula people freely choose using a self-directed learning design (Gureckis & Markant, 2012; Markant & Gureckis, 2014) and which of these features was most predictive of test success. This question is motivated in part by a striking pattern in the self-regulated learning literature: learners’ intuitions about effective study strategies are often misguided, tending to favour easier, more fluent approaches such as rereading even when more effortful strategies yield better outcomes (R. A. Bjork et al., 2013; Kornell & Bjork, 2007). Next, we moved beyond this correlational approach, measuring the impact of curricula that graduated, stabilised, or randomised difficulty along the two axes. Finally, because learning is often most successful in a ‘zone of proximal development’ (Vygotsky, 1978) or ‘Goldilocks zone’ of intermediate challenge (Kidd et al., 2012; Ten et al., 2021), we included experiments in which the curriculum adapted to learner progress in either concept discovery or implementation

To preview our results, we find a systematic dissociation between the curricula that promote concept learning and the curricula that people choose to adopt. When given a choice, participants tend to graduate their own learning progress by adjusting the complexity of concept discovery. By contrast, we found that successful concept learning is promoted via the converse principle: graduating the difficulty of concept implementation. These results held over multiple experiments and generalised to a distinct non-spatial task, suggesting they may constitute a general principle for human concept learning.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In total, 1164 participants played a computerised grid world game modelled after an escape room (Fig. 1a). They attempted to navigate an avatar (Pac-Man icon) to a goal (gift icon) using keys that represented moves in the four cardinal directions. The goal was located in a different room and separated from the avatar by a series of walls. To move from room to room, the participant had to grasp the functionality of diverse tools (i.e. to discover concepts): for instance, a key to unlock a door or a catapult to propel the avatar over a wall. How each tool was used had to be discovered by trial and error (for example the key had to be retrieved before the door could be unlocked, and the catapult had to be approached from a specific direction). We manipulated two sources of task difficulty (Fig. 1b-c). Discovery complexity indexes the number of distinct tools included in the task (between 1 and 4 distinct tools, across target and distractor paths; we introduced each new tool in increasing order of empirical difficulty, see Fig. S1). Implementation complexity indexes the number of operations needed to reach the goal (where an operation is the use of a single tool to move between rooms), or the required plan depth. These two variables could be manipulated independently, resulting in a 2D space of levels from which curricula could be sampled (Fig. 1d).

Transfer phase: Participants completed 10 trials at the highest level of difficulty [4,4]. Importantly, the shapes that signalled each tool were swapped with new shapes.

sec.p: To understand what makes a successful learning trajectory, in Exp. 1 we first let human participants choose their own curricula (that is, to engage in self-directed learning (Gureckis & Markant, 2012; Markant & Gureckis, 2014)). Players [n=299] were first familiarized with the 2D complexity space (Fig. 1e, familiarization phase) and then instructed to choose the difficulty of each training round, by clicking on a square (Fig. S2) within a spatial visualisation of the 4 x 4 complexity grid (training phase). Following training, participants’ learning outcomes were probed in a separate test phase followed by a transfer phase, where the visual mappings of tools were swapped. During test and transfer participants were financially incentivised to perform as well as possible; performance during the training phase had no effect on remuneration. Average performance (% solved rounds) improved across familiarisation and training and stabilised at ~80% at test, but transfer performance was much more variable across participants (Fig. 2a; transfer data reported in Fig. S5).

sec.title: What curricula do people choose during self-directed learning of concepts?
sec.p: In Exp.1 we first studied the curricula that participants chose during self-directed learning. We tackle this problem via three distinct analyses. Firstly, we visualise the marginal probabilities of choosing each difficulty level in the 4 x 4 grid (Fig. 2b). This measures the frequency with which each level was sampled but ignores information about the sequence in which they were chosen. The distribution of level selections has a pronounced bimodality, particularly later in training (Q3-4), with both the easiest level [1,1] and the hardest level [4,4] being selected most often (we saw no convincing evidence that these selections were made by disjoint groups of people; Fig. S3). On average, participants tended to select higher discovery levels relative to implementation levels over the course of training (Fig. 2c, main effect of complexity type on selected level: b(implementation) = -0.06, p<.001).

Secondly, we plot a vector for each participant corresponding to the overall change in selection probability in the 4 x 4 grid, both within and between quartiles of the experiment (Fig. 2d). For example, for a participant who chose to gradually increase both the discovery complexity and implementation complexity in equal measure, this vector would point at +45° both locally (within quartile) and globally (between quartile).

Deviations towards horizontal (vertical) indicate a tendency for participants to adjust the curriculum along the axis of concept discovery (implementation). We thus tested for positive and negative deviations from 45° both within and between quartiles. We found that both local (14.8°±0.65°)) and global vectors (3.73°±2.93°) were titled towards horizontal (Rayleigh Test of Uniformity in circular data, local vector against 45°, statistic = 0.83, p< .001; global vector against 45°, statistic = 0.52, p< .001). This effect grows over the course of training, with participants adjusting concept discovery preferentially in later quartiles (Q1=19.7°, Q2=15.9°, Q3=13.9°, Q4=9.53°, Watson-Williams test for homogeneity of means of circular data, F (3,1192)=12.51, p< .001; linear effect of quartile on vector angle degree: b(quartile) = -3.26, p<.001). Despite some variability (especially in the global vector) this indicates that participants are prone to respond by adjusting the complexity of concept discovery more than concept implementation (Fig. 2e).

Thirdly, we examined the first order (trial-wise) transitions that participants chose to make from level to level. These can be visualised in a 16 x 16 matrix, which plots the probability of transition between each of the possible levels and every other (Fig. 3a). Squares above the main diagonal indicate transitions to more difficult levels, whereas those below the main indicate transitions to easier levels. Visual inspection suggests that participants’ level transitions tend to cluster along the main diagonal, which means participants tend to repeat the current level (proportion on-diagonal transitions, mean±s.e. = 27.3%±1.26%); they also preferentially transition upwards (proportion above diagonal transitions, 44%±1.12%, proportion below diagonal transitions, 28.7%±0.97%, permutation-based t-test, p<.001).

sec.p: Importantly, however they also populate the parallel offset diagonals (especially above the main diagonal), which correspond to adjacent discovery (blue dashed lines) and implementation (orange dashed lines) levels. In Fig. 3b we plot the relative fraction of transitions that repeat a level, or move incrementally up or down a difficulty level, along the dimensions of discovery and implementation complexity. Regression analysis revealed that participants were more likely to transition between consecutive discovery levels relative to consecutive implementation levels across both upwards and downwards transition directions (main effect of complexity type on proportion transitions across: b(implementation)=-0.02, p=.001; follow-up permutation-based t-test comparing upwards transitions by complexity type: p<.01; downwards: p<.01).

We also measured how level adjustments depended on whether the previous trial was successful or not. In Fig. 3c, we plot the proportion of trials where the participant increased the level of discovery and implementation complexity against previous trial success. Participants were more likely to increase the discovery level relative to implementation level following a successful trial (interaction effect between complexity type and previous trial success: b=-0.07, p<.001, follow-up permutation t-test between proportion of trials adjusted up following correct trial by complexity type: p<.01), but tended to decrease discovery and implementation complexity similarly according to trial success (p=.10). In other words, after successfully completing a level, participants felt emboldened to discover new concepts, rather than practising implementation of the concepts they have already discovered in more complex action plans.

In sum, we found that for our grid world game (1) the overall direction of adjustment in a self-directed curriculum tends towards concept discovery, rather than concept implementation, (2) this was the case both for trial-to-trial adjustment and across the study, and (3) this adjustment was conditional on previous trial success or failure.

sec.title: What curricula predict successful learning of concepts?
sec.p: Next, we asked which curriculum choices are associated with learning success (this is a correlational approach; we use a causal manipulation in later experiments). First, we used regression to quantify the relationship between curriculum choices and learning success. Paradoxically, even though participants tended to prioritise training on levels with higher discovery complexity, those who trained on levels with higher implementation complexity progressed most over training, indicated by the difference between their performance in the familiarization phase and the test phase (Fig. 4a, we report standardized coefficients for comparability of effect sizes across metrics, β (implementation) = 0.26, p <.001, β (discovery) = 0.09, p=.26; residuals were normally distributed and homoscedastic, Shapiro-Wilk W=0.99, p=.18; Breusch-Pagan BP=0.88, p=.83).

Participants whose transitions resembled the ones implied by the implementation-first curriculum performed better at test (orange, high RDM similarity > low); this was not true in the case of the discovery-first curriculum.

sec.p: We further probed what curriculum choices made during training predicted better test performance overall. Since test performance is a proportion bounded between 0 and 1, we used ordered beta regression with participant random intercepts, which natively handles bounded outcomes without requiring normality or homoscedasticity assumptions. Here, we found positive associations between choosing higher levels on both complexity axes and performing better on the test phase overall (b(implementation) = 0.39, 95% credible interval (CrI; the Bayesian analogue of a confidence interval) = [0.23, 0.52]; b (discovery) = 0.35, 95% CrI [0.22, 0.49]), with higher difficulty test conditions showing correspondingly lower performance as expected (Fig. 4b).

Second, we probed how the trial-wise transition data related to test performance. We categorised trials into six classes according to whether discovery, but not implementation was graduated up [d+ i=] or vice versa [d= i+], or their downwards equivalents [d- i=] and [d= i-], and trials where there was no movement [d= i=], lumping all other trials together into a final category. We then compared test performance of participants that had few or many transitions of each type, based on median split (Fig. 4c). We found that more successive transitions upwards in implementation complexity (permutation t-test: test performance for high proportion [d= i+] > for low proportion [d= i+], p<.05) were associated with higher test performance, but this was not the case for discovery complexity (p=.30). That is, better test performance was associated with training trajectories that increased the implementation complexity between successive levels whilst holding discovery complexity constant.

Next, we designed a theoretical curriculum in line with this principle, traversing the 2D complexity space in vertical sweeps (implementation-first curriculum, Fig. 4d, top right panel), practicing each level 3 times before progressing to the next. We contrasted this curriculum with a discovery-first curriculum, which privileged adjustments to discovery complexity (i.e. horizontal transitions, Fig. 4d, top left panel). For clarity, we can conceive of each of these training trajectories as a double loop, with inner and outer components. In the discovery-first curriculum, the inner loop circles rapidly through the 4 discovery complexity levels, and the outer loop circles slowly through the 4 implementation complexity levels.

We calculated whether participants whose training choices resembled this curriculum performed better at test, by computing the similarity of each participant’s transition matrix to a discovery-first curriculum an implementation-first curriculum. In Fig. 4d, we visualize test performance for a median split of participants according to the similarity metric (beta coefficient) for each curriculum. Test performance was higher for participants whose choices resembled the implementation-first curriculum (Fig. 4d, bottom right panel, permutation t-test on median split of betas: p<.01) but not the discovery-first curriculum (Fig. 4d, bottom left panel; p=.16).

Previous work has suggested that in order for a learner to progress, they should choose training levels that are sufficiently challenging given their current mastery of the task, but not so difficult that they are impossible to achieve (or that fall in the ‘Goldilocks zone’ (Kidd et al., 2012; Ten et al., 2021)). We assessed this using computational modelling of each learner’s current mastery of the task and found that whilst both challenging and Goldilocks-zone selections were positively associated with test performance, adding them as predictors to the base regression model did not improve overall model fit. We report those analyses in Fig. S4.

sec.title: Randomized controlled curriculum comparisons
sec.p: Building on these results, in Exp. 2-3 we assessed the causal relationship between curriculum choices and learning success by randomising participants into either discovery-first or implementation-first curricula, as described above and depicted in Fig. 1d. Crucially, both curricula traversed the full 2D complexity space and trained each level an equal number of times, but differed in the order in which levels were presented. As in Exp. 1, the training budget was 48 rounds, and so participants completed 3 rounds of each of the 16 levels. Below, we report data from the training and test phases. Transfer results (null across all curricula) are in Fig. S5.

The findings from Exp.1 imply that the implementation-first curriculum should lead to more successful learning outcomes. Across two cohorts (Exp. 2 [n=104], presented in (Dumbalska et al., 2023), and Exp. 3 [n=98], which was a replication), this is what we found. Performance was higher in the implementation-first curriculum during training (Fig. 5a, left panels, permutation-based t-test: Exp. 2, p<.001; Exp. 3, p<.001), as well as on a subsequent test phase (Fig. 5a, right panel, permutation-based t-test: Exp. 2, p<.05; Exp. 3, p<.05). The difference in test accuracy between conditions was 13%-14.7%, amounting to a curriculum advantage of approximately half a standard deviation (Cohen’s d = 0.47-0.53, moderate effect size). Performance was also higher on “training probe” trials, which were training levels that coincided in time across curricula (permutation-based t-test: Exp. 2, p<.05; Exp. 3, p<.001; Fig. 5a, middle panel). In a further experiment, we also asked whether the curriculum effects endured, by repeating the experiment except with test delayed by a week (Exp. 4, [n=177]). Here, performance on training (permutation-based t-test: p<.01) and probe (p<.01) trials was once again higher under the implementation curriculum, but test was not (p = 0.44) ([n=91], see Fig. S6 for attrition analyses), implying that this effect of curriculum may be relatively short lived.

sec.p: In Exp. 2-4 the curriculum was fixed, and participants progressed through the training trajectory at the same pace irrespective of their performance. A more personalized approach to curriculum design adapts the training pace to each learner, such that the progression over the trajectory matches their ongoing performance, allowing some learners to progress through the curriculum faster than others. In Exp. 5 [n=94] we made level transitions performance-contingent (Fig. 5b, left panels top illustrate adaptive curricula). The two curricula were the same as before - implementation-first vs discovery-first -- but levelling up only happened following a correctly-solved round, and failing to solve a round resulted in bumping the level down. Charting the training trajectories of learners in Exp. 5 shows that those in the implementation-first condition progressed faster and reached farther in the curriculum (Fig. 5b, left panels show average level over the course of training; main effect of curriculum on level reached: b(implementation-first)=.26, p<.001, interaction effect of curriculum and trial number on level reached: b(implementation-first=.02, p<.001). As in the fixed curricula, they also did better during training (permutation-based t-test: p<.01) and when tested following training (Fig. 5b, right panel plots performance: p<.05, Cohen’s d=0.45).

One possibility is that participants failed to organize their self-directed learning in line with the implementation-first curriculum because they found it diff icult or unpleasant. To test this, we solicited ratings of participants’ engagement, immersion, absorption and enjoyment of the task, feelings considered the hallmarks of flow (Method following (Melnikoff et al., 2022), 5.9±.05 on a 7-point Likert scale). Participants reported experiencing more flow-like states in the implementation-first curriculum (Fig. 6; regression analysis of flow ratings obtained prior to the completion of the test phase in Exp. 4, main effect of condition on ratings b(implementation-first)=.31, p<.05). Indeed, in line with existing work on flow that highlights its benefits for performance (Engeser & Rheinberg, 2008; Schüler, 2007), we found that participants’ self-reported flow experiences were associated with better learning outcomes on the test phase (across the curriculum and self-directed experiments: b(implementation-first)=.05, p<.001) for a 1- point increase in self-reported flow, test accuracy increased by 5 percentage points.

sec.title: Dissociating the effects of level repetition and adjustment
sec.p: The implementation-first curriculum has two key features: it (1) repeats the discovery complexity of the task and (2) adjusts the implementation complexity of the task. Are both features necessary for the success of the curriculum, or can we eliminate either one of them at no cost? To test this, we carried out a control experiment (Exp. 6, [n=300]), where we systematically varied whether each complexity dimension was adjusted, repeated, or chosen randomly, yielding 6 distinct conditions (results in Fig. 7a-b). These include the implementation-first curriculum (which involves repeat-discovery and adjust-implementation components) and discovery-first curriculum (adjust-discovery repeat-implementation components) that we have already encountered, but also four curricula in which levels from one dimension were sampled randomly.

Middle panel: as above, but for the adaptive random implementation-first curriculum. Bottom panel: accuracy in the test phase did not differ meaningfully between curricula, but there was a trend for an adaptive random discovery-first curriculum advantage.

sec.p: We used ordered beta regression to model participant learning outcomes on test as a function of adjustment and repetition dimensions (both with levels concept, strategy or neither). That is, we labelled which complexity axis each of the 6 curricula adjusted or repeated and regressed test performance on the resulting 2 x 3 factors. This analysis showed that repeating improves test performance both in the case of discovery levels (b(discovery-repeated) = 0.51, 95% CrI [0.19, 0.82]) and implementation levels (b(implementation-repeated) = 0.35, 95% CrI [0.04, 0.67]). Adjusting implementation levels showed a positive but less certain association (b(implementation-adjust) = 0.30, 95% CrI [-0.02, 0.63]), while adjusting discovery levels did not (b(discovery-adjust) = 0.16, 95% CrI [-0.16, 0.47]). Thus, whilst both curriculum components matter for learning outcomes -- the implementation-first curriculum outperforms both the control curriculum that only repeats discovery (permutation-based t-test: p<.001), and the control curriculum that only adjusts implementation (p<.05) -- the repeating effect appears to have a more pronounced impact. Indeed, model comparison confirmed that a model featuring only the repeating factor fits the data as well as a model featuring both repeating and adjusting factors (LOO elpd_diff = -0.3, SE = 1.9).

We confirmed the importance of repeating concept discovery levels in a further control experiment (Exp. 7, [n=92]) that paralleled the adaptive curriculum in Exp. 5. Here we again graduated the progression along a target source of complexity but permuted --rather than stabilized -- the other source of complexity (schematic in Fig. 7c, top and middle panel). This adjustment eliminated the curriculum advantage we observed in Exp. 5 (Fig. 7c, bottom panel, permutation-based t-test: p=.17), underscoring the importance of repeating the complexity of concept discovery during learning.

sec.title: Does the curriculum advantage generalize across tasks?
sec.p: Our evidence suggests that an implementation-first curriculum leads to faster and more effective learning. But are our results restricted to the specifics of the grid world task or do they generalize across settings? We addressed this by developing a new task that was markedly different in surface properties from the gamified maze used in Exp. 1-7, but retained its basic structure, where a series of steps were taken to reach a goal. Instead of spatial navigation, in Exp. 8 [n=100], we asked participants to perform sequences of binary operations, cloaked under the guise of a potion-creation cover story. To solve the task, participants had to apply ingredients (concepts) to a cauldron. Ingredients changed the colour of the potion in the cauldron (binary variable, green or purple) in distinct ways that were unknown to the participant a priori and had to be discovered (Fig. 8a). Different ingredients may turn the potion one colour (e.g. green), swap the current colour, etc. (just as tools had different effect in the spatial navigation problem). We manipulated the complexity of concept discovery and implementation in the same way as in Exp. 1-7: by increasing the number of concepts (or potion ingredients, in ascending order of difficulty) and the depth of the plans required for a successful solution. As before, concept implementation reflected the sequencing of the game concepts to reach a signalled goal: here, combining ingredients to achieve the requested potion colour.

Despite major differences in the surface properties of the new task, we observed the same pattern of results as before: participants performed better in the implementationfirst condition during training and probes (Fig. 8b, permutation t-test: training p<.05, probes, p<.05) although test did not quite reach significance (p=.07). This lends support to the idea that focussing on graduating the difficulty of concept implementation during learning offers a general principle of complex task learning.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Across eight experiments involving both a spatial and a nonspatial paradigm, we studied how curricula should be designed for effective learning of complex tasks. Our results reveal two principles of successful active learning. Learners should discover concepts slowly and progressively, focussing on mastering their use before attempting to discover new concepts. This approach, which we call an implementation-first curriculum, leads to better learning outcomes in all of the studies reported here. This is a counter-intuitive finding for learners. When allowed to freely choose, participants adopted a very different strategy, prioritising the discovery of new concepts over their use. This has the important implication that it may be possible to correct this tendency in new learners, in a way that will enhance their overall learning success.

Our findings build on and extend the blocking versus interleaving literature (Carvalho & Goldstone, 2014; Dekker et al., 2022; Kornell & Bjork, 2008) by dissociating two distinct dimensions of concept learning -- discovery and implementation -- and showing that optimal sequencing principles differ across them. Repeating levels with similar discovery complexity is beneficial: work in category learning has shown that blocking opportunities to explore instances of the same concept together (e.g. pronunciation rules for French words) may emphasise shared commonality across exemplars and aid acquisition of abstract representations (Carpenter & Mueller, 2013; Carvalho & Goldstone, 2014). In our games, as in the real world, examples of the same concept differ on many dimensions --a door may come in different colors and in different locations across rounds of the game; stabilizing the concept discovery dimension during learning may aid generalization in future training rounds by highlighting the concept’s context-independent nature -- the systematicity of the transition afforded by each tool and the shape that signals it. This may at first appear to contradict findings from educational psychology -- blocking has been shown to come at a cost in some contexts (E. L. Bjork & Bjork, 2011a), and when learning mathematical formulae or categorizing painting styles, interleaving outperforms blocking (Kornell & Bjork, 2008; Rohrer & Taylor, 2007). However, this difference owes to our operationalisation of discovery complexity: in each successive discovery level, we add concepts rather than swap them, so earlier concepts remain relevant throughout.

Gradually increasing the difficulty of concept implementation is consistent with the idea that curricula should ‘start small’ (Elman, 1991; Skinner, 2019) and that learners benefit from deliberate practice (Ericsson & others, 2006). Computational models of complex task learning have emphasised that planning depth, rather than formation of new heuristics, predicts increasing competence (measured by Elo score) (Van Opheusden et al., 2023) suggesting that using concepts in more sophisticated ways (implementation complexity) is both a consequence and cause of successful learning.

Perhaps our most striking of our findings is that in our task, what people choose to do and what they should do to learn successfully are diametrically opposed. Although graduating the difficulty of concept implementation strongly predicts success, participants freely choose to adjust the number of concepts required to solve a problem instead. This cannot be explained by the implementation-first curriculum being more difficult or unpleasant; we find that participants report greater flow in that condition. Past work has shown that learners’ intuitions about their own learning can be surprisingly misguided: more effortful strategies are often mistaken for less effective ones (R. A. Bjork et al., 2013; Kirk-Johnson et al., 2019; Zechmeister & Shaughnessy, 1980), and feelings of fluency are misleading because difficulty is actually desirable during training (E. L. Bjork & Bjork, 2011a; R. A. Bjork et al., 2013; Kornell & Bjork, 2008). Indeed, when given the choice, learners tend to gravitate toward easier, more fluent strategies such as rereading, even when more effortful approaches like retrieval practice yield better outcomes (Kornell & Bjork, 2007). The same pattern may apply here: solving rounds at low implementation complexity may feel productive because they are completed faster, but practicing harder implementation levels yields better outcomes.

We found no curriculum effects in the transfer phase, and effects disappeared when the test was delayed by a week. One possibility is that the implementation-first advantage is narrow and limited. However, performance was much more variable in both the transfer condition (and to some extent with delay), suggesting individual differences in knowledge retention may obscure curriculum effects. Consistent with this, imputation analyses in the delayed test experiment revealed a significant curriculum advantage approximately half the size of the immediate test effect, suggesting the effect may persist but decay, and that our study was likely underpowered to detect it at delay. It is also possible that 48 trials are insufficient to foster lasting, generalisable representations. Indeed, concept learning appears to be a necessary but not sufficient condition for generalisation: all participants who generalise have learnt well, but not all who learn well generalise. Our supplementary analyses (Fig. S4) suggest that only one variable -- the tendency to neither over- nor under-challenge oneself during training (the Goldilocks effect (Kidd et al., 2012; Ten et al., 2021)) -- was weakly predictive of successful transfer, tentatively implicating metacognition in the ability to generalise knowledge. As a more general limitation to our work, even though our findings were obtained in two complex online tasks that already exceed the naturalistic richness of typical laboratory paradigms, it remains to be seen whether the implementation-first advantage scales to longer training regimes and real-world learning contexts.

Learning by doing has emerged as an effective way to boost educational outcomes (Yannier et al., 2021) and level the playing field for disadvantaged learners (Theobald et al., 2020). Our work contributes a basic science understanding of the principles that underlie successful active learning: progress and outcomes benefit when opportunities to discover a new concept are grouped together and the difficulty of implementation is gradually dialled up.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: All studies were carried out online. We recruited participants on Prolific Academic. All participants had an acceptance rate >80% on the crowdsourcing platform. The gender composition of our sample was 42% female, 57% male and 1% nonbinary or other, and the age composition -- [18-20]: 6%, [21-30]: 49%, [31-40]: 26%, [41-50]:12%, [51-60]: 5%, and [61+]: 2%. We aimed for 50 participants per condition in the controlled studies (Exp. 2-7) to allow us to detect a medium effect size with 80% power. Final numbers of participants vary slightly from that goal due to a small number of participants failing to provide data due to self-reported technical issues.

Each experiment took 20-60 minutes and was self-paced. Participants were remunerated for their participation on average £10 per hour as well as a performance-based bonus that was proportional to percentage rounds solved in the task (Exp.1: test and transfer phase only, Exp. 2-8: across all phases). All participants provided written consent and the study was approved by the Central University Research Ethics committee, R50750/RE001.
Data and analysis files are available in the OSF repository for the project: https://osf.io/gfxy7/.

sec.title: Escape room task (Exp. 1-7)
sec.p: In escape room experiments, participants were given minimal instructions regarding the task:

p.italic: “Your goal is to move the avatar to the present “[/ gift]”. Press the arrow keys to move the avatar. If you get stuck, press n to move on to the next round (new game).”

sec.p: Only participants in the self-directed experiment (Exp.1) were alerted of the structure of the training and the test phase. This was necessary to instruct them regarding the incentive structure of the experiment; i.e., so that they would be incentivized to select training levels that would allow them to learn best in order to acquire a bonus based on performance at a later stage of the task. Participants in Exp. 2-7 were not given any information about the structure of the task; to make performance salient, the screen featured a “total points” tracker, where each successfully solved round added 5 points and each unsuccessful round deducted 5 points from a participants’ total.

The task comprised a 15x15 square grid. The grid was separated out by 6 walls (grey squares) in 16 evenly sized rooms totalling 9 squares each (3x3). Keyboard input (arrow keys) allowed the participant to navigate an avatar, signalled by a yellow sector shape, across non-wall squares. Game tools (concepts) were denoted by colored shapes, occupying some of the squares on the grid. Shapes and colors were randomly allocated to each tool and counterbalanced between participants. A demo of the game is available here: [https://tsvetomira-dumbalska.github.io/projects/escape-room-demo/]. The tool set comprised of doors, keys, teleporters, levers, portals and catapults. Each tool allowed the participant to transition between rooms with a specific function. Doors (squares in the demo) would allow a participant to move between adjacent rooms, but only if the participant had picked up the key (triangles) in a corresponding color. Stepping on a teleporter (circle) would move the participant to the location of a teleporter of the corresponding color. Portals (club symbol) function in the same way, but only after a lever (heart) has been pressed. Catapults would propel a participant over a wall, but only when approached in the correct direction.

The game featured 16 (4 x 4) different difficulty levels, along two factors: discovery and implementation complexity. Discovery complexity corresponded to the number of concepts that could be included in the grid. At discovery level 1, all tools on the grid comprised of doors and keys (the easiest concept, Fig. S1). At discovery level 2, we introduced teleporters, and so the grid featured teleporters (which were always included in the target path during training), but could also feature doors and keys (which had been previously introduced). That is, we randomly drew the tools on the grid from the available pool of already introduced concepts, with the constraint that the newly introduced tool type needed to be utilized to reach the goal. Concepts were introduced in ascending order of difficulty over the different discovery levels (i.e. door first, catapult last, difficulty was estimated in piloting). Implementation complexity corresponded to the number of tool interactions (or successful transitions between rooms) required to reach the goal. In each level there was a single successful trajectory through the layout (target path) and two distractor paths, one diverging from the spawn room of the avatar, one from the goal room. This meant that the problem could not be solved through a simple heuristic (follow the single available trajectory forward / backward from goal room) but required engagement in planning. All levels also included unusable distractor objects for visual clutter.

sec.title: Potions task (Exp. 8)
sec.p: Participants were given minimal instructions regarding the task:

p.italic: You need to create a potion that matches the goal color in the bottle.
You can add an ingredient to your potion by clicking on it. You will always have a choice of 2 options for the first ingredient.
Some potions will have more than 1 ingredient and you will see multiple transparent ingredients to follow your first choice.
When potions have more than one ingredient, you will need to use all ingredients in the order presented.

sec.p: The task featured a cauldron (signalling the current potion color), a vial (signalling the goal potion color), and a series of ingredients. Participants were always given a choice between 2 options. The total number of ingredients depended on the implementation level: at implementation level 1, participants could add only 1 ingredient (choice of 2 possible options); at implementation level 4, participants could add 4 ingredients (choice of 2 possible options for the first ingredient). Participants had to click on each ingredient in successive order, starting with their choice for the first ingredient. The ingredients to follow were presented with higher transparency level, so participants could plan ahead.

The game featured 16 (4 x 4) different difficulty levels, along two factors: discovery and implementation complexity. Discovery complexity corresponded to the number of unique ingredients that could be included in the grid. We randomly drew the possible ingredients for each level from the available pool of already introduced ingredients (introduced in the order [keep, switch], [green], [purple], [goal]). Implementation complexity corresponded to the number of ingredients that needed to be added to the potion. In each level, the participant was given a choice between 2 options for the first ingredient and the following ingredients (if any), were visually indicated on the screen (Fig. S7).

The participant could observe the effect of each ingredient addition on the color of the potion in the cauldron. We included animation effects (rotating sparkles, 500ms) following each ingredient click to slow down the task, ensuring participants could observe the effect of the ingredient on the potion color and prevent them from clicking through the task too quickly.

sec.title: Exp. 1.
sec.p: The experiment comprised 4 phases: familiarization (9 trials), training (48 trials), test (37 trials), and transfer (10 trials). 299 participants completed the study across three waves of data collection.

Participants were told that the study comprised 2 parts. In the first part, we invited them to familiarize themselves with the game (familiarization phase) and complete 48 rounds (training phase) where they select the level of difficulty for each round. We told participants that they should “select the difficulty so that [they] best learn how to play the game”. We informed participants that the second part would assess how well they’ve learnt to play the game (test and transfer phase) and that their bonus payment would depend on how many rounds they solve successfully here.

In the familiarization phase, at the start of each trial, participants saw a 4 x 4 grid. The two axes of the grid were labelled “Difficulty type A” and “Difficulty type B”; these referred to discovery and implementation complexity (counterbalanced). We aimed to familiarize participants with the two complexity axes by providing them examples of levels that spanned the full range of the complexity space, as well as the core of the grid; this also served the additional purpose of allowing us to assess pre-training abilities on the game. In each trial, participants were invited to click on a greyed-out node on the grid, which would select a trial of the corresponding level. All participants completed the following 9 levels in the order [conceptual, strategic]: [1,1], [1,4], [1,1], [4,1], [4,4], [2,2], [2,3], [3,2], [3,3]. Written instructions accompanied each level drawing the participants’ attention to which complexity axis was changed between adjacent trials, and which was held constant (Fig. S2).

Following the 9 familiarization trials, participants were allowed to freely select which level to complete on each of the 48 training rounds. Level choice was indicated on the same grid as in familiarization. Participants were invited to take a couple of minutes break after training before continuing to the second part of the experiment.

In the test phase, we shuffled all 16 levels of the game and presented participants with two rounds at each level, as well as 5 additional rounds at level [4,4]. In the transfer phase, we swapped the shapes that signal each tool with a new set of shapes; transfer rounds were at the highest complexity level [4,4]. This allowed us to assess generalization of knowledge.

sec.title: Exp. 2-3.
sec.p: In Exp. 2 and 3, we implemented a controlled experimental design. Participants were randomly allocated to one of two curriculum conditions that determined the order of training rounds. The experiments comprised of three phases: training (48 trials), test (8 trials), and transfer (8 trials). During training, all participants completed 3 rounds of each complexity level. That is, across conditions, participants completed the same levels, what differed was the order. sec.title: Exp. 4.
sec.p: The procedure for Exp. 4 followed that of Exp. 2-3, but the test and transfer phases were administered a week later. Due to the staggered temporal design, we recorded high attrition rates, despite warning participants to only register for the experiment if they would be willing to complete both parts in the indicated time frame (Fig. S6).

We initially recruited 50 participants, but as a large portion of them failed to complete part 2 in the allowed time window (24 hours a week after their initial participation), we launched a second wave of recruitment.

sec.title: Exp. 5, 7.
sec.p: The procedure for the adaptive curriculum experiments followed the general structure of Exp. 2-3. The experiments comprised of three phases: training (32 trials), test (8 trials), transfer (8 trials). Participants were randomly allocated to an adaptive implementation-first or discovery-first curriculum. In Exp. 5, the sequencing of levels for each curriculum followed the same logic as in Exp. 2-3, but transitioning to the next level was contingent on successfully completing the current round. If the current round was successfully completed, on the next round, the participant completed the following level; if the current round was unsuccessful, on the next round, the participant completed the previous level. In Exp. 7, in the implementation-first curriculum, the implementation complexity was increased following a successfully solved trial (and decreased following an unsuccessful trial), but discovery complexity was always randomly assigned on each round.

sec.title: Exp 6.
sec.p:
The procedure for the control curricula in Exp. 6 followed that of Exp. 2-3. The experiments comprised of three phases: training (48 trials), test (8 trials), transfer (8 trials). Participants were randomly allocated to one of 6 conditions. Half of the conditions probed the effect of different components of the implementation-first curriculum and half -- of the discovery-first curriculum:

sec.title: Exp. 8.
sec.p: Here, we mirrored the design of Exp. 2-3. The study comprised a training (48 trials) and a test phase (8 trials). Participants were randomly allocated to an implementationfirst or discovery-first curriculum. During training, all participants completed 3 rounds of each complexity level, in the same order as in Exp. 2-3. The test phase comprised 8 trials of the highest difficulty.

sec.title: Analyses
sec.p: Unless otherwise noted, group differences between curriculum conditions were assessed using permutation-based t-tests (10,000 permutations), which make no distributional assumptions and are robust to the bounded, proportion-valued nature of accuracy data. Effect sizes are reported as Cohen’s d. Regression analyses used linear mixed effects models (LME; nlme package in R) with participant random intercepts, except where outcomes were proportion-valued (i.e. test and transfer accuracy), for which we used ordered beta regression (ordbetareg package), which natively handles bounded outcomes without requiring normality or homoscedasticity assumptions. Fixed effect predictors were standardized (z-scored) prior to fitting where noted to allow comparison of effect sizes across metrics. Model comparisons used leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV; loo package), which estimates out-of-sample predictive accuracy via the expected log pointwise predictive density (elpd). A difference is considered meaningful when |elpd_diff| > 2 * SE. All analyses were conducted in R; data and analysis code are available at the OSF repository for the project.

sec.title: Movement vector analysis
sec.p: To characterise the direction of participants’ trial-by-trial curriculum choices, we computed a movement vector for each trial as the angular direction of the step taken in the 2D complexity space. Specifically, for each trial t, we computed the change in discovery complexity (Δd) and implementation complexity (Δi) relative to the preceding trial, and calculated the angle of movement as arctan(Δi, Δd). An angle of 0° corresponds to pure movement along the discovery axis (horizontal), 90° to pure movement along the implementation axis (vertical), and 45° to equal movement along both axes. Perparticipant vectors were averaged within and across quartiles of training to yield local (within-quartile) and global (between-quartile) movement vectors. We tested whether the distribution of mean angles deviated significantly from 45° — which would indicate a bias toward one complexity axis — using the Rayleigh test of uniformity for circular data (circular package in R), with the expected mean direction set to 45°. Changes in vector angle over the course of training were assessed with the Watson-Williams test for homogeneity of circular means across groups, and a linear mixed effects model of vector angle as a function of training quartile.

sec.p: All behavioral data and analysis code are deposited at https://osf.io/gfxy7/ and are publicly available.

sec.title: Figure S1: Estimating concept difficulty
sec.p: We estimated the difficulty of the 4 concepts during piloting. Thirty-four participants were invited to complete 80 rounds of the escape room game; they were financially incentivized to perform as well as possible. Each round consisted of a single-step problem (implementation level = 1) and featured only 1 concept (i.e. all tools on the grid were the same type). We split the 80 rounds evenly between concepts (20 rounds each) and randomly interleaved their presentation order. As a proxy for concept difficulty, we considered both accuracy and reaction time.

For accuracy, we calculated the proportion of rounds that participants solved for each concept. Performance was highest for doors, followed by teleporters and portals (at about the same accuracy level), followed by catapults (all Bonferroni-adjusted comparisons significant at p<.05, other than portal against teleporter comparison, which has an unadjusted p=.3). We additionally compared the first RT (time to first step in each round) by concept. We assumed that more difficult concepts would require the participant to think longer about what to do. Here, we found that RTs were shortest for doors and teleporters (at about the same timing), followed by portals, followed by catapults. Based on these results, we estimated that doors < teleporters < portals < catapults in terms of difficulty.

The nodes were selected to demonstrate the effect that changing the level of each axis has on the game.

sec.title: Figure S3: Level selections
sec.p: In our main results, we observed that the distribution of level selections has a pronounced bimodality, particularly later in training, with both the easiest level [1,1] and the hardest level [4,4] being selected most often. To ascertain whether these selections were made by disjoint groups of people, we carried out singular value decomposition (SVD) analysis, which permits the identification of factors contributing to the pattern of level selections across participants. We did this by flattening the 4 x 4 level selection matrix for each participant into a vector of values and constructed a large matrix of level selections, where each row indexed an individual participant and each column - the discovery and implementation complexity level. SVD produces a set of basis functions, or principal components, and allows us to examine the amount of variance explained by them in the empirical data. This, in turn, illustrates the structure of level selections across participants.

Our results show that the pattern of level selections were highly variable across participants: we needed the first 10 (out of 16) principal components (PC) to explain 75% of the variance in the data. Across many of these components, we find that participants select levels [1,1] and [4,4] in similar proportion, except for PC2, PC 5 and PC6, which jointly account for 23% of the variance in the data.

sec.title: Figure S4: Modelling individual learning progress
sec.p: Previous work has suggested that in order for a learner to progress, they should choose training levels that are sufficiently challenging given their currently mastery of the task, but not so difficult that they are impossible to achieve. In the next analyses, we studied how curriculum choices (and their resulting learning success) depended on the degree of mastery of the task that a participant has so far achieved.

To characterise participants’ curriculum choices in terms of their ongoing mastery of the task, we built a trial-by-trial model of learning progress. The model maintained a 4×4 mastery matrix, where each cell represented the estimated probability of correctly solving the corresponding complexity level. On each trial, the relevant cell was updated using a delta rule: a correct response increased estimated mastery for all levels at or below the current level (reflecting the assumption that success at a harder level implies competence at easier ones), while an incorrect response decreased mastery for all levels at or above the current level. Two summary scores were derived from the mastery matrix on each trial. The ‘challenge’ score captured the tendency to choose levels with low current mastery (i.e. levels the participant had not yet mastered), computed as the negative of the mastery estimate for the chosen level. The ‘Goldilocks score ‘captured how close the mastery of the chosen level was to the median mastery across all 16 levels, computed as the negative absolute deviation from the median — higher scores reflect choices in the intermediate zone of challenge (or the ‘Goldilocks zone’). Both scores could be computed from the full 4 x 4 mastery matrix (combining both complexity axes) or marginalized separately over discovery and implementation axes using two 4x1 vectors tracking mastery along each dimension independently. Per-participant summary scores were obtained by averaging trial-wise scores over the training phase.

We used this model to ask how curriculum choices predicted better learning outcomes. Although adding Goldilocks and challenge scores to a model of curriculum choices did not substantially improve overall model fit (leave-one-out cross-validation expected log pointwise predictive density difference, LOO elpd_diff = -3.8, SE = 41.5), both showed credible positive associations with test performance within the model (b(Goldilocks) = 0.14, 95% CrI [0.01, 0.26]; b(challenge) = 0.47, 95% CrI [0.21, 0.75]). This suggests that the tendency to seek out challenging but reachable levels is associated with better learning, even if this effect is modest relative to the overall difficulty of levels chosen.

Curiously, when we probed knowledge generalization on a subsequent transfer phase of the task, where the visual mappings of game tools changed but the underlying rules remained the same, a different pattern emerged. Only the Goldilocks effect was associated with successful transfer (b(Goldilocks) = 0.19, 95% CrI [0.03, 0.34]) when we control for differences in learning outcomes (i.e., when we include test accuracy for the highest difficulty test rounds in the regression as a competitive predictor, b (test accuracy) = 0.56, 95% CrI [0.39, 0.72]), potentially suggesting different mechanisms for successful knowledge acquisition and generalization.

sec.title: Figure S5: Transfer phase results
sec.p: Exp. 2-7 included a transfer phase where tool mappings (i.e. the shapes that signalled each concept) were randomly swapped with new shapes, thus permitting investigation of whether the two curricula led to differential degrees of knowledge generalization. We found no difference between the discovery-first and implementation-first conditions (permutation-based t-tests: Exp. 2, p=.84; Exp. 3, p=.97; Exp. 4, p=.92; Exp. 5, p=.95; Exp. 6, p=.91; Exp. 7, p=.96). This null finding echoes our results from participants’ selfdirected learning in Exp. 1, where we didn’t find associations between training choices and generalization performance (other than making selections at an appropriate level of challenge, i.e. not under- or over-challenging oneself -- Goldilocks effect).

sec.title: Figure S6: Attrition in Exp. 4
sec.p: In Exp. 4 we strove to investigate the long-term retention effects of our curricula. To this end, we divided the training phase and test / transfer phases into two separate sessions, separated by a week. We aimed to recruit approximately 50 participants per condition but observed a high degree of attrition: only half of the recruited participants returned for session 2 (51%). And so, we were obliged to launch a second wave of recruitment (totalling 177 participants), resulting in 89 / 48 participants for the discovery-first condition and 88 / 43 participants in the implementation-first condition for the training / test phase respectively. Average performance for training phase, training probes and test phase are plotted below.

Due to the high drop-out rate, we carried out imputation analysis with Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations (R package MICE) that allowed us to estimate the expected test performance of participants who failed to return for the test phase. Imputing missing values, resulted in a statistically significant contrast between our curriculum conditions (permutation-based t-test, p<.05). We plot the imputed curriculum comparison below. The estimated mean difference (9 percentage points, Cohen’s d = 0.30) in the imputation analysis is approximately half the one we observe in the main experiment (47% lower), so it is possible that we were underpowered to detect differences between conditions here.

sec.title: Figure S7: Potions task
sec.p: In the potions task, participants needed to add ingredients sequentially by clicking on them. The currently available ingredient(s) were fully opaque (100% opacity), ingredients to follow were slightly transparent. Below is an example of implementation level 4, where the participant needed to add 4 ingredients to the potion. In this trial, the starting colour is green and the goal is green. At the first step, the participant has the choice between a root (that swaps the current colour) or a stone (that always turns the potion green). The participant can see the subsequent ingredients: an herb (that keeps the current color), a root, and an herb. Given the effects of ingredients 2, 3, and 4, the correct choice for the first ingredient is root, which would turn the potion purple. Then, the second ingredient - the herb - would preserve the purple color of the potion; the third ingredient - the root - would swap it back to green, and the final ingredient - the herb - would preserve the green color, resulting in a green potion at the final stage.

After each selection, there was a .500ms animation of rotating sparkles over the potion and the potion assumed the color implied by the selected ingredient. This was intended to slow the task down and allow the participant more time to consider the effects of each ingredient.

sec.title: Supplementary Note on Analytic Deviations from Pre-registration
sec.p: The self-directed learning experiment (Exp. 1) was conducted as part of a student project and pre-registered on the Open Science Framework prior to data collection (two preregistrations: February 2024: https://osf.io/k45tz/, April 2024: https://osf.io/z529f, covering a planned replication wave). The randomised controlled experiments (Exp. 2-8) were not pre-registered.

The experimental method followed the preregistration. Note that we have adjusted the labelling of the two axes from ‘conceptual’ and ‘strategic’ complexity to ‘concept discovery’ and ‘concept implementation’ for clarity. The analysis plan differed from the reported analyses in the paper in the following respects:

sec.title: Analyses conducted as pre-registered (confirmatory)
sec.p: We pre-registered and report PCA analyses on level selections in the Supplement (we used SVD, which is mathematically equivalent to PCA). We pre-registered analyses of curriculum progression, examining how participants adjusted complexity levels trial-by-trial conditional on performance. We report trial-wise transition analyses and the finding that participants preferentially adjusted discovery rather than implementation complexity and that higher performance is associated with adjustments in implementation complexity. We pre-registered and report transition matrices within meaningful diagonals and transition types, as well as contrasts according to performance. We pre-registered computational modelling of Goldilocks and challenge scores (inverse of mastery) and report those in the Supplementary materials, as they did not improve overall model fit relative to a base model (for similar reasons, we omit the subjective difficulty axis factorization). We preregistered and report the analysis of effects on learning progress [test - familiarization] in the main text and generalization [transfer] in the Supplemental file.

sec.title: Analyses that changed in operationalisation
sec.p: We pre-registered delta complexity scores; the reported angular movement vector approach addresses the same question (how participants navigate the 2D complexity space) but uses a different operationalisation that we judged more interpretable and better suited to characterising directional bias. Our pre-registered analyses on learning outcomes [test and transfer] did not specify that we would use ordered beta regression; we made this choice post-hoc to appropriately handle the bounded nature of proportion outcome data, we found that our results were not sensitive to this modelling choice.

sec.title: Analyses that were attempted but unsuccessful
sec.p: The pre-registration described plans to train a recurrent neural network on participants’ trial sequences to predict test performance, and to invert it to identify the optimal curriculum. This analysis was implemented but the model overfit severely due to insufficient sample size (N = 299 sequences of 48 trials), failing to learn generalizable sequence representations. The analysis was therefore uninformative and is not reported.

sec.title: Analyses reported but not pre-registered
sec.p: The flow ratings analysis and the curriculum similarity scores were developed after data collection and were not pre-registered.

body.p: This valuable study evaluates how different learning curricula in a complex planning task impact performance. The authors provide convincing evidence across eight behavioral studies that practicing increasingly difficult examples of a concept before moving to the next concept benefits immediate performance, despite participants having a preference for the reverse - learning new concepts before practicing. However, there is incomplete evidence for claims about relevance to real-world learning settings, as the curriculum effects did not persist across a delay or support transfer to new problem types. The paper will be of interest to researchers studying learning curricula, problem solving, planning, and education.

This work uses a compelling pairing of controlled task design with rich, naturalistic behavior. It is ambitious, with eight experiments, both correlative and causal demonstrations, delayed assessments, and generalization of the phenomena to a very different domain.

The stated goal of the paper is to understand how learning different curricula "promote successful learning of complex tasks in human adults," which is a very broad scope. The evidence for generalization to a non-spatial task is compelling, but the structure of the two tasks is isomorphic, and it is still difficult to claim likely generalization to all complex tasks. For example, one could wonder to what extent demands of the task or online setting may have explicitly or implicitly encouraged participants to prefer trials that can be completed more quickly, biasing them towards choosing discovery transitions. Is it possible that they believed that the experiment might end more quickly if they chose trials that were faster to complete?

This paper investigates how curricula should be structured to support learning in complex tasks, focusing on the distinction between concept discovery (learning new components) and concept implementation (learning how to use them in increasingly complex sequences). The main finding is that participants tend to prioritize discovering new concepts, even though learning outcomes are better when they instead practice implementing known concepts in increasingly complex ways.

A major strength of the paper is the experimental paradigm. The grid-world task is a novel way of independently manipulating two dimensions of complexity that are often confounded: the number of concepts that need to be learned and the complexity with which those concepts must be deployed. Participants have to learn how the underlying tools operate and use them in different configurations, which provides an interesting setting for studying variability in how individuals structure their own learning. Additionally, the experiments progress from correlational analyses of self-directed learning, to randomized experimental comparisons of curricula, and finally to transfer and adaptive curriculum tests. Overall, this paper addresses an important question about whether the complexity of concept discovery versus implementation is better for structuring learning.

The main concern is that the paper's conclusions do not seem to fully match the evidence. The authors present the results as identifying a relatively general principle of complex learning, such that we should master a concept's implementation before introducing new concepts. There was no implementation-first advantage in the transfer phase, and when testing was delayed by one week, the curriculum difference was no longer detectable. Although the implementation-first curriculum improves immediate performance within the constraints of these experimental paradigms, it is less clear that it produces more generalizable learning. Additionally, it is not sufficiently clear how the "flow" measure was created, what "flow" means in the context of subjective task experience, or more broadly in everyday learning, and what inferential role the measure plays in the paper.

The authors report findings from a set of experiments that compare learning outcomes from two broad classes of training regimens. The first, concept discovery, emphasizes the identification of task components. The second, concept implementation, emphasizes the procedural deployment of task components. Learners tend to self-schedule the former, but task performance and performance on an immediate test are supported by the latter.

The authors address a novel research question with clear application value. The experiments that are reported in the manuscript are effectively designed to answer the research questions of interest. However, as I will expound on below, the authors ultimately misinterpret their findings.

This manuscript makes no mention of the distinction between learning and performance (e.g., Schmidt & Bjork, 1992; Soderstrom & Bjork, 2015). It is well-known in the human learning literature that valid tests of learning are ones that entail a separation of context from an initial acquisition phase. This separation may be temporal (i.e., a delayed test) or feature-based (i.e., a test of transfer on novel iterations of a task). In any case, contextual differentiation between test and acquisition is critical to provide an accurate assessment of learning. To the authors' credit, they do report results from both a delayed test and tests of transfer. However, they do not appropriately interpret the results of those tests, which demonstrate no impact of training schedule on learning. They instead rely on findings from immediate tests to support their claims that graduated concept implementation supports learning. In truth, concept implementation is neither preferred by learners nor beneficial to learning. These findings are accordingly quite limited in terms of generating insights for effective training conditions.

Compounding my primary concern above, I will note that the authors report fitting Bayesian multilevel models (MLMs) to their data, yet rely extensively on analyses of participant means (e.g., permutation t-tests) when a proper MLM would suffice, and in fact would be more appropriate. Bayesian MLMs are an incredibly flexible and robust analytic tool (e.g., Fiechter, 2024), and I would have liked to have seen a more comprehensive approach in this manuscript.
